title: 3 Clever Things You Can Do With an Old Amazon Kindle
gist: A light how-to piece describing three community-built projects that repurpose a retired Amazon Kindle: a Spotify Connect remote via the web app Kindlify.co, an E-Ink smart home dashboard built from developer Matt Healy's published scripts, and a literary clock cycling 1,440 pre-made quote images. No market analysis — the only durable signal is that the Kindle's built-in browser plus third-party APIs give old e-readers a second life without any official Amazon support.

insights.claim: An old Amazon Kindle can be turned into a Spotify playback remote by opening Kindlify.co in the e-reader's built-in web browser and connecting Spotify credentials, with the Kindle on the same Wi-Fi network as the playback device.
insights.speaker: David Nield
insights.so_what: Third-party web apps can extend closed consumer hardware without vendor cooperation, extending device lifespans beyond the manufacturer's upgrade cycle.
insights.locator: Turn Your Kindle Into a Spotify Controller

insights.claim: The Kindle-Spotify hack stores no music locally and runs no official Spotify app — it works purely through Spotify Connect, which lets one device control playback happening on another.
insights.speaker: David Nield
insights.so_what: Spotify Connect functions as an open control surface that lets any browser-capable device become a controller, widening Spotify's hardware footprint at zero cost to Spotify.
insights.locator: It all works through the magic of Spotify Connect

insights.claim: A retired Kindle's E-Ink screen can be converted into a smart home display pulling weather forecasts, calendar entries, to-do lists and delivery status reports, using scripts published by developer Matt Healy.
insights.speaker: David Nield
insights.so_what: E-Ink dashboards built on discarded hardware compete directly with purpose-built smart displays, a niche any vendor selling low-refresh screens should watch.
insights.locator: Turn Your Kindle Into a Smart Home Display

insights.claim: The smart display project's data sources are constrained to platforms that allow third-party connections, and it requires building a custom website plus a hand-cut frame — making it the most involved of the three Kindle projects.
insights.speaker: David Nield
insights.so_what: API openness is the binding constraint on the DIY hardware-reuse ecosystem; platforms that close their APIs kill these projects.
insights.locator: The information you display is entirely up to you

insights.claim: The Kindle literary clock project displays a different book quote mentioning each specific time of day, requiring 1,440 static images — one per minute — all of which have already been prepared and published along with the scripts.
insights.speaker: David Nield
insights.so_what: Pre-packaged asset libraries are what lower DIY project friction from impossible to weekend-scale — the reusable pattern behind hobbyist hardware adoption.
insights.locator: Turn Your Kindle Into a Literary Clock

insights.claim: The literary clock deliberately hides the book title and author on each time quote so the display doubles as a quiz, with answers revealed by pressing the Kindle's screen.
insights.speaker: David Nield
insights.so_what: Minor design detail, but illustrates that hobbyist repurposing competes on delight rather than utility — the same axis premium consumer hardware sells on.
insights.locator: A nice touch is that you don’t get to see the name of the book
